title: Joint Tenancy, Tenancy in Common, and Severance
subtitle: The four unities, and the four ways a joint tenancy is broken
objectives: State the distinguishing features of a joint tenancy and a tenancy in common, including the right of survivorship
Apply the four unities test to determine whether a joint tenancy is even possible on given facts

Apply the four recognised methods of severance — statutory notice, an act operating on one's own share, mutual agreement, and course of dealing — to a fact pattern, including cases of partial severance

leadingAuthorities.role: Legal title can only ever be held as a joint tenancy; sets out the statutory mechanics of severance in equity
Source of the three non-statutory modes of severance: act on one's own share, mutual agreement, course of dealing
Negotiations towards a buy-out, even if never completed, can amount to mutual agreement or course of dealing sufficient to sever
A s 36(2) notice severs once validly served, regardless of whether the recipient ever reads it or the sender changes their mind

whyThisMattersTemplate.default: Severance questions are graded on precision, not general understanding — the difference between a full mark and a half mark is usually whether you spotted which of four narrow doctrines applies, and to which share. Where the profile shows knowledge outpacing application, this note appears: 'You know the four unities and the four modes of severance — this lesson is about telling them apart under pressure.'

profileHooks.weakApplication: You've scored well recalling the unities and the modes of severance in the abstract. The test pool below leans hard on application: expect fact patterns that require you to identify which mode of severance is in play, and what share results.
profileHooks.weakKnowledge: Slow down through Parts 1 and 2 and make sure you can list all four unities and all four modes of severance without prompting — the later application questions assume you already have the checklist by heart.

overview.hook: Two friends buy a flat together as joint tenants. Eighteen years later, one of them dies suddenly, having never got round to changing her will to leave her half to her children. It doesn't matter — the will has nothing to sever, and the whole flat now belongs to the survivor. Now change one fact: three years before she died, she posted a single letter to her co-owner. That letter, whether or not he ever opened it, would have changed everything.

parts.heading: Two ways to own together
parts.voice: taxonomic — establishes the two categories as a strict binary before any nuance is allowed in
body: Land co-owned by two or more people is held one of exactly two ways: as joint tenants, or as tenants in common. There is no third option, and the difference between them is not cosmetic — it decides who ends up owning the property when one co-owner dies.

Joint tenants are treated, in the eyes of the law, as a single collective owner. No individual joint tenant holds an identifiable 'share' that can be pointed to, valued on its own, or left by will — each simply holds the whole, together with the others. When one dies, nothing passes under their will or on intestacy: the property is just owned by one fewer person than before. This is the right of survivorship, and it operates automatically, overriding whatever the deceased's will says.

Tenants in common, by contrast, each hold a distinct, quantifiable share — a fraction of the whole, which may or may not be equal. That share is an asset in its own right: it can be sold, mortgaged, or left by will, and it does not pass automatically to the other co-owners on death.

One structural rule underlies everything that follows: since 1925, the legal estate in co-owned land can only ever be held as a joint tenancy, by up to four trustees, on trust for whoever owns the equitable interest. Those equitable owners may hold between themselves as joint tenants or as tenants in common. This lesson is entirely about the equitable position — because that is where severance operates.

components.definition: The automatic rule that on the death of a joint tenant, their interest simply ceases to exist and the surviving joint tenants own the whole property between themselves — nothing passes under the deceased's will or intestacy.

components.text: A legal estate is not capable of subsisting or of being created in an undivided share in land.
elements: No legal tenancy in common is possible
Legal title to co-owned land is always a joint tenancy
Held by up to four trustees on trust for the equitable owners

interaction.prompt: Aisha and Ben buy a house together as joint tenants in equity. Aisha dies without a will, survived by two children. Who now owns Aisha's interest in the house?
options: Ben alone — by survivorship, nothing passes on Aisha's death
Aisha's children, under the intestacy rules, as tenants in common with Ben
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right. Survivorship overrides intestacy just as completely as it overrides a will — there is nothing left in Aisha's estate to pass to anyone.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Not under a joint tenancy. Survivorship means Aisha's interest doesn't survive her at all — it simply vests wholly in Ben. Her children would only inherit if the joint tenancy had been severed before her death.

parts.heading: The four unities: a pass/fail checklist
parts.voice: structural — presents the unities as a strict test students should apply mechanically, reference style
body: Equity will only recognise a joint tenancy where four conditions — the four unities — are all satisfied at the moment the co-owners acquire their interests. Miss one, and a joint tenancy cannot arise at all: the co-owners must hold as tenants in common, regardless of what anyone intended.

Unity of possession: every co-owner is entitled to possession of the whole property, not a physical portion of it. This unity is shared by both joint tenancy and tenancy in common — its absence means the land isn't co-owned at all, it's simply divided into separate plots.

Unity of interest: each co-owner's interest must be identical in extent, nature and duration — the same size of estate, the same kind of estate (for example, all fee simple), for the same period. A fee simple sitting alongside a life interest fails this unity immediately.
Unity of title: each co-owner must have acquired their interest under the same document or act — the same conveyance, the same act of adverse possession, and so on.
Unity of time: each co-owner's interest must have vested at the same moment.

Where all four unities are present, and nothing displaces the presumption, equity treats the co-owners as joint tenants. Where any one unity is missing, only a tenancy in common is possible — and severance, the subject of the rest of this lesson, simply has nothing left to do.

components.label: The four unities checklist
points: Possession — every co-owner is entitled to possess the whole, not a physical share
Interest — every co-owner's interest is identical in extent, nature and duration
Title — every co-owner acquired their interest under the same document or act
Time — every co-owner's interest vested at the same moment

interaction.prompt: Tap the fact that shows one of the four unities is missing in this arrangement.
interaction.scenarioText: David and Elena take a conveyance of a house on the same day, in the same document, each named as beneficial owners. David is expressed to take a fee simple interest, while Elena is expressed to take only a life interest in the property.
tappableSpans: David is expressed to take a fee simple interest
Elena is expressed to take only a life interest
interaction.correctSpan: Elena is expressed to take only a life interest
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Exactly. Possession, title and time all match here — same conveyance, same day. But a fee simple and a life interest are not the same kind and duration of estate, so unity of interest fails and David and Elena cannot be joint tenants.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Possession, title and time are all fine on these facts — same document, same day, both entitled to possess the whole. Look for the fact that makes David and Elena's interests different in kind or duration from each other.

parts.heading: Severance by notice: the statutory route
parts.voice: precise — walks through the statute element by element, then shows how a hard case tested it
body: The first and most reliable way to sever a joint tenancy in equity is the one Parliament provided. Section 36(2) of the Law of Property Act 1925 lets any equitable joint tenant sever unilaterally, without anyone else's consent, simply by giving the other joint tenants notice in writing of their desire to sever.

Two features make this route distinctive. First, it requires no agreement and no cooperation — one joint tenant can sever against the wishes of all the others, converting their own interest (and only their own interest) into a tenancy in common. Second, and this is the point examiners return to, the notice takes effect on service, not on receipt or on actual awareness.

Kinch v Bullard tested exactly this. A wife, terminally ill, posted a notice of severance to her husband intending to sever their joint tenancy before she died. Before he had read it, she had a change of heart and tried to destroy the letter — but it had already been delivered through the letterbox. The court held the notice had already taken legal effect the moment it was validly served; her later change of mind, and the fact her husband never actually read it before her death, made no difference at all. The joint tenancy had already been severed.

The lesson generalises: once a s 36(2) notice is properly served — left at the last known address is normally enough, under the deeming provisions the section borrows from s 196 LPA 1925 — severance has happened. It cannot be undone by regret, and it does not depend on the other party's state of knowledge.

components.text: ...where a legal estate is vested in joint tenants beneficially, and any tenant desires to sever the joint tenancy in equity, he shall give to the other joint tenants a notice in writing of such desire...
elements: A legal estate vested in joint tenants beneficially
One tenant desires to sever the equitable joint tenancy
Notice in writing of that desire
Given to the other joint tenant(s) — effective on valid service, not on receipt or agreement

components.factsShort: A wife posted a s 36(2) notice to her husband, then tried to intercept and destroy it before he read it.
components.ratioShort: A s 36(2) notice severs the moment it is validly served — the sender's later change of mind, and the recipient's ignorance of it, are both irrelevant.

expanded.facts: Mrs Kinch and Mr Bullard held the matrimonial home as equitable joint tenants. Mrs Kinch, seriously ill, instructed solicitors to send a notice of severance under s 36(2) so that her share would pass under her will rather than to her husband by survivorship. The notice was delivered through the letterbox. Before Mr Bullard read it, Mrs Kinch reconciled with him and destroyed the letter herself before he saw it. She died shortly afterwards, and the question was whether the joint tenancy had already been severed.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The court held that service of a s 36(2) notice is governed by the deeming provisions of s 196 LPA 1925: a notice is validly served once it is left at the recipient's last known place of abode, whether or not it subsequently comes to their actual attention. Once served, the notice takes immediate legal effect and cannot be revoked unilaterally by the person who sent it.
expanded.significance: Kinch v Bullard is the leading illustration that severance by notice is a formal, mechanical act, not a communication that depends on the other party actually reading or agreeing to it. It also shows severance can outlive the sender's own change of heart — a sobering point for students who assume severance requires ongoing mutual intent.

interaction.prompt: Which element of s 36(2) LPA 1925 is satisfied simply by posting a letter through the recipient's letterbox, even if the recipient never opens it?
options: Notice in writing given to the other joint tenant — service is complete on valid delivery, not on the recipient reading it
The desire to sever, which must be read aloud to the other joint tenant in person
Agreement of all joint tenants, which the letter is evidence of
interaction.feedbackCorrect: Right — s 36(2) requires the notice to be given, and delivery to the last known address satisfies that whether or not it's ever actually read. There is no requirement of agreement or of the recipient's awareness.
interaction.feedbackIncorrect: Look again at what s 36(2) actually requires: writing, and giving it to the other tenant. Neither reading it aloud nor obtaining agreement is any part of the test — service alone does the legal work.

parts.heading: Three more doors, all from one 1861 case
parts.voice: menu-style — sets out three remaining routes as parallel options, then tests the line between two of them that students most often blur
body: Severance by notice is a twentieth-century statutory creation. The other three recognised methods are much older, and come from a single case: Williams v Hensman, decided in 1861, which is still the starting point whenever a s 36(2) notice hasn't been used.

First, an act of a joint tenant operating on their own share. If a joint tenant sells, mortgages, or otherwise alienates their own equitable interest, that act severs their share immediately and unilaterally — without needing to tell, let alone obtain the agreement of, the other joint tenants. Only that share is severed; the remaining joint tenants stay joint tenants as between themselves.

Second, mutual agreement between all the joint tenants to sever. This needs no particular form, and — crucially — it does not need to be a binding, legally enforceable contract. An agreement that later falls through can still have severed the tenancy, if genuine mutual intention to hold separately is what it shows.

Third, a course of dealing sufficient to intimate that the parties treated their interests as separate shares. No express agreement is needed here at all — just conduct from which a court can infer that the parties no longer regarded themselves as joint tenants.

Burgess v Rawnsley shows how thin the line between the second and third can be. Two elderly acquaintances bought a house as joint tenants; one later negotiated with the other to buy out her share, and they agreed a price in principle — but the sale never completed. The Court of Appeal held severance had nonetheless occurred: either the negotiated agreement itself was a mutual agreement to sever (even though never formally concluded), or, if that was too generous a reading, the negotiations were at minimum a course of dealing showing both parties no longer treated the property as jointly held. Either route got to the same destination.

components.factsShort: Two joint tenants negotiated a price for one to buy out the other's share; the sale never completed, but negotiations were held enough to sever.
components.ratioShort: Negotiations towards a buy-out, even one that never completes, can amount to mutual agreement to sever, or at least a course of dealing evidencing that the parties no longer treated their interests as joint.

expanded.facts: Mr Honick and Mrs Rawnsley bought a house as joint tenants, apparently on the mistaken shared assumption that they might marry. The relationship did not develop as either hoped. Mrs Rawnsley later agreed, in principle, to sell her interest to Mr Honick for £750, but she then raised the price and the sale fell through entirely. After Mr Honick died, the question was whether his interest had passed by survivorship to Mrs Rawnsley, or whether the joint tenancy had already been severed by the earlier negotiations.
expanded.judgmentExtract: The Court of Appeal held that an agreement to sever need not be a specifically enforceable contract — an oral agreement in principle, even one later abandoned, is capable of showing the mutual intention required. In the alternative, the course of the parties' negotiations was itself conduct from which severance could be inferred, independent of whether any concluded agreement was ever reached.
expanded.significance: Burgess v Rawnsley loosened what earlier authority had suggested was a stricter requirement, and confirmed that the second and third Williams v Hensman categories overlap and reinforce each other — a court need not cleanly choose between 'agreement' and 'course of dealing' where the facts support both.

interaction.prompt: Which scenario is most likely to sever a joint tenancy by mutual agreement or course of dealing?
interaction.scenarioA: Two joint tenants exchange emails negotiating a price for one to buy the other out. They agree a figure in principle, but the deal never completes because financing falls through.
interaction.scenarioB: One joint tenant privately tells a friend she'd like to leave her share to her daughter one day, but never raises the subject with her co-owner.
interaction.explanation: A mirrors Burgess v Rawnsley precisely: negotiated agreement towards separate ownership, even if never completed, evidences mutual intention or at least a course of dealing. B involves no communication to the other joint tenant at all — a private, unshared wish cannot sever, because severance by agreement or dealing requires something passing between the joint tenants, not a secret intention held by one alone.

parts.heading: Putting it together: partial severance
parts.voice: direct — closes with the trap examiners rely on most, testing whether students track the effect on the group as well as the individual
body: A question that catches out even well-prepared students: what happens to the co-owners who are left behind when only one joint tenant severs?

The answer follows directly from what severance actually does. Severance converts one person's interest from a joint tenancy into a tenancy in common — it says nothing about anyone else's interest. Where three or more people hold as joint tenants and one severs (by notice, or by an act on their own share), the severing party becomes a tenant in common of their share. The remaining co-owners, however, continue to hold as joint tenants between themselves as to the rest — right of survivorship intact among them — while also being tenants in common with the person who severed.

This means a single co-ownership can end up as a hybrid: part joint tenancy, part tenancy in common, simultaneously. It is not an all-or-nothing event, and treating it as one is the single most common error in exam answers on this topic.

components.title: Severance in a group: who is affected
components.description: How severance by one joint tenant among several affects the others.

nodes.label: Three or more equitable joint tenants; one severs (notice or act on own share)
Severing party: now a tenant in common of their fractional share
Remaining co-owners: still joint tenants as between themselves as to the rest
Result: a hybrid — tenancy in common as to the severed share, joint tenancy as to the remainder

components.textAlternative: When one joint tenant among three or more severs, only their own interest is converted into a tenancy in common. The remaining co-owners continue to hold as joint tenants between themselves as to the rest of the property. The overall result is a hybrid: a tenancy in common as to the severed share, sitting alongside a joint tenancy among the co-owners who did not sever.

interaction.prompt: Fatima, Grace and Hassan hold a house as equitable joint tenants. Fatima sells her equitable interest to her cousin Layla. What is the effect on Grace and Hassan's relationship with each other?
options: They become tenants in common with each other too, splitting into three equal shares alongside Layla
Layla becomes a tenant in common as to a one-third share; Grace and Hassan remain joint tenants as between themselves as to the remaining two-thirds
The whole co-ownership collapses automatically and the property must be sold
interaction.explanation: Severance by an act on one's own share only ever affects that share. Fatima's sale severs her interest and creates a tenancy in common between Layla and the others as to that one-third — but Grace and Hassan never did anything to sever their own relationship, so they remain joint tenants between themselves, complete with survivorship, as to the remaining two-thirds.

testPool.prompt: Name the four unities that must all be present for a joint tenancy to arise in equity.
acceptableAnswers: unity of possession, interest, title and time
testPool.modelAnswer: Unity of possession, unity of interest, unity of title, and unity of time — all four must be present at the moment the co-owners acquire their interests.

testPool.prompt: Can the legal estate in co-owned land ever be held as a tenancy in common?
options: No — since 1925, legal title to co-owned land can only be a joint tenancy
Yes — the legal estate can be split into shares just like the equitable interest

testPool.prompt: Which of the following is NOT one of the four unities?
options: Unity of possession
Unity of interest
Unity of consideration — each co-owner must have paid an equal price
Unity of time
testPool.trapExplanation: Equal financial contribution is not a unity at all, and is not even required for a joint tenancy — two people can be joint tenants having paid wildly unequal amounts towards the purchase, provided the four real unities (possession, interest, title, time) are satisfied.

testPool.prompt: Under the right of survivorship, does a deceased joint tenant's interest pass under their will?
options: No — it never forms part of their estate at all; it simply ceases to exist
Yes, unless the will says otherwise

testPool.prompt: Under s 36(2) LPA 1925, when does a notice of severance take legal effect?
options: On valid service on the other joint tenant(s) — not on their actually reading it or agreeing to it
Only once all joint tenants sign a formal deed of severance
Only once the notice is registered at the Land Registry

testPool.prompt: Put the events of Kinch v Bullard in the order they happened.
items: Mrs Kinch instructs solicitors to send a s 36(2) notice to her husband
The notice is delivered through the letterbox
Mrs Kinch reconciles with her husband and destroys the letter before he reads it
The court holds the joint tenancy had already been severed on delivery

testPool.prompt: In the passage below adapted from Burgess v Rawnsley, highlight the sentence that states the ratio.
testPool.passage: The parties had negotiated, in some detail, for one to buy the other's share, and had reached agreement on a price, though the transaction was never completed. An agreement to sever need not be a specifically enforceable contract; it is enough that it shows a mutual intention that the parties' interests should thenceforth be held separately. That the deal later collapsed does not undo the severance already effected.
testPool.ratioSentence: An agreement to sever need not be a specifically enforceable contract; it is enough that it shows a mutual intention that the parties' interests should thenceforth be held separately.

testPool.prompt: Why did the notice in Kinch v Bullard remain effective even though Mrs Kinch destroyed it before her husband read it?
options: Because destroying a document is itself a criminal offence, which the court would not assist
Because severance by notice takes effect on valid service, and cannot be undone by the sender's unilateral change of mind afterwards
Because Mr Bullard had a right to be told about the notice by a third party regardless
testPool.trapExplanation: The criminal law point is irrelevant to this civil property question, and nothing in the case turns on a third party informing Mr Bullard. The ratio is narrower and more mechanical: once served, a s 36(2) notice has already done its legal work.

testPool.prompt: Tap the fact that shows unity of time is missing from this arrangement.
testPool.scenarioText: Omar and Priya buy a flat together under a single conveyance, each taking an identical fee simple interest with full rights of possession. Four years later, Omar's sister Nadia is added to the legal and beneficial title by a fresh deed of variation, taking an identical fee simple share to the others.
tappableSpans: identical fee simple share to the others
testPool.explanation: Nadia's interest is identical in nature (unity of interest is fine) but it vested years after Omar and Priya's, under a different document — so unity of time (and, separately, unity of title) fails as between Nadia and the original pair.

testPool.prompt: Which scenario amounts to severance by an act operating on one's own share?
testPool.scenarioA: A joint tenant mortgages her equitable interest to a bank to raise money, without telling her co-owner.
testPool.scenarioB: A joint tenant tells his co-owner he is thinking about selling one day, but takes no further steps.
testPool.explanation: Mortgaging one's own equitable interest is a classic act operating on one's own share under Williams v Hensman — it severs unilaterally, with no need to inform or obtain agreement from the other joint tenant. Merely mentioning a future possibility, with no act and no agreement, severs nothing.

testPool.prompt: Two joint tenants, Sanjay and Tomasz, jointly sign a single document stating clearly that from now on they wish to hold the property as tenants in common in equal shares. Has the joint tenancy been severed?
options: Yes — this is a mutual agreement to sever, effective even without the formality of a s 36(2) notice
No — only a s 36(2) notice can ever sever a joint tenancy
No — mutual agreement must be recorded in a deed to have any legal effect
testPool.explanation: Mutual agreement is a free-standing, non-statutory route to severance under Williams v Hensman. It requires no particular formality — a clearly expressed, genuinely mutual intention to hold separately is enough.

testPool.prompt: Nia, Owen and Priti hold a cottage as equitable joint tenants. Owen, without telling the others, declares himself bankrupt and his equitable interest vests in his trustee in bankruptcy. Six months later Owen dies. Analyse the effect on ownership of the cottage.
factsToOrder: Nia, Owen and Priti are equitable joint tenants
Owen is declared bankrupt; his interest vests in his trustee in bankruptcy

scaffolds.support: Full model IRAC answer shown, with each fact mapped to Issue / Rule / Application / Conclusion
Rule and Issue given; student drags facts into Application and writes Conclusion
No scaffold; student writes full IRAC unaided

modelAnswer.issue: Whether Owen's bankruptcy severed the joint tenancy before his death, and if so, what happens to his share.
modelAnswer.rule: The vesting of a joint tenant's equitable interest in their trustee in bankruptcy (by operation of insolvency law) is treated as an act operating on that tenant's own share, severing the joint tenancy as to that share under the first Williams v Hensman category.
modelAnswer.application: Owen's bankruptcy vested his interest in his trustee before his death, severing his share from the joint tenancy at that point. Nia and Priti remain joint tenants as between themselves as to the remaining two-thirds. Owen's now-severed one-third share, held by the trustee, does not pass by survivorship on his later death — it remains an asset of his bankruptcy estate, distributable to his creditors.
modelAnswer.conclusion: The joint tenancy was already severed as to Owen's share before he died; his subsequent death has no effect on that share, which stays with his trustee in bankruptcy, while Nia and Priti remain joint tenants of the rest.

testPool.prompt: A joint tenant posts a s 36(2) notice, which is delivered to the other joint tenant's last known address while that person is abroad for six months and never actually sees it before returning. Is the joint tenancy severed?
options: Yes — service at the last known address is sufficient under the deeming provisions; actual awareness is not required
No — severance requires the other joint tenant to actually read the notice
No — the sender must wait until the recipient returns before the notice can be served at all
testPool.explanation: As Kinch v Bullard confirms, service is complete on delivery to the last known address, regardless of whether or when the recipient actually reads it. Absence abroad makes no difference to the notice's legal effect.

testPool.prompt: Does severance by an act on one's own share require the agreement of the other joint tenants?
options: No — it operates unilaterally and needs no notice, agreement or awareness from the others
Yes — the other joint tenants must consent before the act can sever anything

debriefConfig.trapSummary: The most common mistake in this lesson's test items is treating severance as an all-or-nothing event for the whole group. It almost never is: severance by notice or by an act on one's own share affects only the severing party's share, leaving the remaining co-owners as joint tenants between themselves. Always ask 'severed as to whose share?' before answering.
